title: A Number After a Double Reversal
summary: An integer is reversed by inverting its digits.
statement: An integer is reversed by inverting its digits. Reversing an integer twice should yield the original integer if no leading zeros are retained during the first reversal. Given an integer, reverse it to get the first reversed integer, then reverse that result to get the second reversed integer. Return true if the second reversed integer matches the original integer, otherwise return false.
constraints: Decimal reversal discards leading zeros in the reversed representation.
Return whether reversing num twice recovers num.
reference_solution:
def same_after_double_reversal(num):
    return num==0 or num%10!=0
hints: Only zeros at the end of the original can be lost as leading zeros after the first reversal.
Zero itself is unchanged; every positive number must have a nonzero last digit.
A nonzero final digit becomes a nonzero leading digit and survives both reversals; a trailing zero is irrecoverably discarded.
editorial: A nonzero final digit becomes a nonzero leading digit and survives both reversals; a trailing zero is irrecoverably discarded.

tests.explanation: Neither reversal loses a significant zero, so the original number is recovered.
The first reversal drops two zeros, so the second reversal cannot restore 1800.
